lines.text: # Host Control: the companion listens, plugins define the commands

lines.author: Máté Molnár

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: feat(examples): Host Control demo Deck App, docs, and agent-check
lines.text: **Host Control** lets a **Deck App** ask a nearby computer to run a typed command. Draft PR #16 designed and built it as one 50-file change: SDK contract, companion CLI, a `sceHttp` client on the Vita, vendored picohttpparser, a rewritten upload server, and an always-on LAN listener that changed the **Runtime Upload** lifecycle. It was closed because it could not be reviewed or rebased. This ADR keeps the parts of that design that held up and drops the rest.

lines.text: Host Control was planned as three slices (#109 wire contract and SDK client, #110 Host Companion CLI, #111 native link and Shell screen). They landed together in one PR on request, as one commit per slice, and the slice boundaries still hold: the SDK client needs neither a Vita nor a companion in its tests, the companion tests against a TypeScript stand-in for the Vita link endpoint, and only the native slice needs the `full` agent-check tier. All three replay the same contract fixtures in `tests/fixtures/host-control/`.

lines.summary: feat(shell): one LAN Listener for upload and link, on from startup
lines.text: The user reads the Vita's address in the VitaDeck Shell and gives it to the **Host Companion**. The companion sends one link request (`POST /link`) with its protocol version, a stable id, its name, and the callback URL where it accepts commands. VitaDeck stores that URL and sends each later command to it as an HTTP POST. The companion is the long-lived listener.

lines.author: Máté Molnár

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: feat(shell): one LAN Listener for upload and link, on from startup
lines.text: **One LAN Listener, on from startup.** `POST /link` is a route on the same **LAN Listener** as **Runtime Upload**, and VitaDeck starts it at boot; the **Shell Listener Entry** turns it off and on. A first version gave links their own listener on 8798 that ran only while the **Shell Host Control Screen** was open, next to an upload listener the user started from the Shell. Setting up a Deck App with a plugin then meant two Shell steps and two addresses before anything worked. Now both `vitadeck dev <vita>` and `vitadeck-host-companion link <vita>` take the same address, with nothing to open first. The cost is exposure: whenever VitaDeck runs, anyone on the LAN can install a Deck App or add a link, until credentials exist (see Deferred).

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: feat(shell): one LAN Listener for upload and link, on from startup

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: feat(shell): one LAN Listener for upload and link, on from startup
lines.text: This is the only option that meets the pairing goal ("type the Vita's address on the computer") without running a session server on the Vita. Steady-state commands need no new native code: Deck Apps already have `fetch()` on libcurl, with completions on a worker thread, on both targets. That makes #16's 650-line `sceHttp` client unnecessary. A new TCP connection per command costs a few milliseconds on a home LAN, which is fine for button presses and for polling a gauge once a second.

lines.text: **Several computers.** VitaDeck keeps up to 4 links, newest first, keyed by the companion's id, so one Deck App can drive several machines (`createHostClient(plugin, { hostId })`) and a relink replaces rather than duplicates. One companion can likewise be linked by several Vitas.

lines.text: Accepted costs:

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: docs(adr): host control sliced delivery and topology (#70)
lines.text: - The companion needs an inbound firewall rule.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: feat(host-control): the companion relinks its Vitas on every start
lines.text: - A stale callback URL (a DHCP change, or the companion restarting on another port) breaks commands until the companion restarts. Each `start` relinks the Vitas it linked with `relink: true`, which only updates a link VitaDeck still has, so a computer forgotten in the Shell is not linked back; VitaDeck answers `unknown_link` and the companion drops that Vita. A Vita that is off is retried every 30 s.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: feat(host-control): computers push events to Deck Apps by long-polling
lines.text: - One request per watching Deck App stays open at the companion, and is renewed every 25 s while nothing happens (see Events).

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: feat(examples): Host Control demo Deck App, docs, and agent-check

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: fix(host-companion): start plugin lifecycles after binding the port
lines.text: **Events: the Vita long-polls the companion.** The computer cannot open a connection to the Vita, but it can hold one the Vita opened. A plugin declares **Host Control Events** next to its commands (`defineHostPlugin(id, commands, { name: event<Data>() })`), and its implementation emits them from a `start(emit)` lifecycle the companion runs while the plugin is loaded. The companion numbers events and keeps the last 100 of each plugin. The built-in `core.events({ plugin, after })` answers at once when there are events after `after`, and otherwise holds the request until the plugin's next event or 25 s, under the Vita fetch's 30 s cap. `watchHostEvents(plugin, onEvent)` in the SDK keeps one such request open, passing the returned `next` as `after`, so an alert reaches the Vita within one network round trip and nothing between two requests is lost. `core.notify` emits a `notice` that every Deck App can watch, which lets a script on the computer (`make && vitadeck-host-companion notify "Build done"`) reach the Vita with no plugin at all. Events are best effort: an `after` from before a companion restart starts over from now, and events beyond a plugin's last 100 are dropped. It needs no new protocol on the Vita, only the existing `fetch()`, which runs each request on its own thread, and one fix: stopping a Deck App cancels its pending fetches through curl's progress callback, so a held request does not stall a reload for 25 s.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: feat(host-control): computers push events to Deck Apps by long-polling

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: feat(shell): one LAN Listener for upload and link, on from startup
lines.text: Considered for events: server-sent events over a streaming response (rejected: the Vita's `fetch()` buffers whole bodies, so it needs streaming in C, for little over long-polling); a WebSocket or a companion-held session with the Vita (option B: the companion dials in and keeps a session; it gives lower per-command latency, but costs a WebSocket client or server, a command queue and reconnect logic in Vita C, the riskiest native work here); and the companion POSTing events to the **LAN Listener** (rejected: it needs a native route from the listener into the running Deck App, the companion to track which Vitas watch what, and credentials first; long-polling needs none of these). Revisit option B only if long-polling proves too slow or too costly on the Vita.

lines.text: ## Commands come in plugins

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: feat(examples): Host Control demo Deck App, docs, and agent-check

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: feat(host-control): built-in plugins, .vdplugin files, vitadeck-host-companion
lines.text: A fixed catalogue in the companion cannot cover what Deck Apps will want (keyboard shortcuts, media keys, a Stream Deck-style grid, sensors and fan control, a T3 Code dashboard), and a generic "run this shell command" endpoint loses types and invites misuse. So commands are grouped into **Host Control Plugins**. A plugin is a typed registry (`defineHostPlugin(id, { name: command<Payload, Result>(guard) })`) that a Deck App imports and bundles, plus an implementation (`implementHostPlugin(registry, implementations)`) that the companion runs. Every request names its plugin and command; the companion validates the payload with the registry's guard, and TypeScript fails a missing or mistyped implementation. `capabilities` lists every loaded plugin, so a Deck App can tell a computer without a plugin (`unknown_plugin`) from an offline one.

lines.text: There is no schema library, since one would ship inside every Deck App bundle. The protocol version covers only the envelope; a plugin changes its own command names when it breaks them.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: feat(host-control): built-in plugins, .vdplugin files, vitadeck-host-companion
lines.text: **Built-in plugins first.** The companion ships the plugins most Deck Apps need, and the SDK exports their registries, so a Deck App that uses only those needs nothing installed beyond the companion. Today that is `core` (`capabilities`, `echo`) and the read-only `systemStats`. Keys and shortcuts, media keys and opening apps or URLs are the next built-ins, and each waits for credentials (see Deferred). Plugins tied to one program, like a T3 Code dashboard, or to one machine, like fan control, stay custom.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: feat(host-control): built-in plugins, .vdplugin files, vitadeck-host-companion

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: feat(sdk): Host Plugins can be authored without a Deck App
lines.text: **A custom plugin lives in a project, with or without a Deck App, and ships as a package, like the Deck App.** The author adds `hostPlugin` (`entry`, optional `files`) to `vitadeck.config.json`: next to a Deck App's `entry` (`create --host-plugin`), or alone in a plugin project (`create --host-plugin-only`) whose `package.json` exports the command registry, so any number of Deck Apps depend on it the way they depend on any package and its users install it once. `vitadeck build` writes the **Host Plugin Package**, a `<slug>.vdplugin` folder with `manifest.json`, the implementation bundled with its npm dependencies and the SDK code it uses into one ES module (`companion.mjs`), and the `files` folder, then zips it to `<slug>.vdplugin.zip` next to the `.vdapp.zip`. It is a folder and a zip rather than one JavaScript file because plugins will carry more than code (scripts, data, native addons a bundle cannot inline); the entry finds them through `import.meta.url`, and the manifest's `schemaVersion` leaves room to grow. The zip keeps no file modes, so a plugin runs a shipped script through its interpreter rather than executing it directly. The user runs `vitadeck-host-companion install <archive>`, which unpacks it into `~/.vitadeck/plugins/<id>.vdplugin`, and a running companion reloads that folder and every `--plugin` path when they change, so `vitadeck dev` plus `start --plugin ./dist` is the author's edit loop. The companion imports the entry by file URL, with a query of its content hash so a rebuild loads fresh instead of from the module cache. It checks the default export's shape (`id`, a `Map` of commands) and a `HostCommandError`'s name and code rather than classes, since each package bundles its own copy of the SDK. The manifest and that shape are the contract between a package built with one SDK version and a companion of another.

lines.text: Considered for custom plugins: npm packages the companion resolves by name (rejected: an author would publish a package per Deck App, and a global companion cannot resolve packages installed elsewhere); one bundled JavaScript file (rejected: it cannot carry anything but code); and serving the implementation from the Vita at link time (rejected: the Vita would push code that the computer runs).

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: feat(host-control): a Deck App's plugin ships as a .vdplugin package and zip
lines.text: **Two CLIs, one per machine role.** `@vitadeck/sdk`'s `vitadeck` builds Deck Apps and Host Plugin Packages; `@vitadeck/host-companion`'s `vitadeck-host-companion` runs on any computer a Vita controls. A single `vitadeck host ...` would make every user install the Deck App build toolchain (Babel, rolldown) to run a server. A second bin in the SDK would also break `npx @vitadeck/sdk`, which works only while the package has exactly one bin. The companion bundles the SDK code it needs and has no dependencies.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: feat(shell): one LAN Listener for upload and link, on from startup
lines.text: The Vita parses exactly one new kind of request: a small JSON link POST with `Content-Length`, answered with `Connection: close`. The upload server became the **LAN Listener** (`src/net/lan_listener.c`) with a `/link` route, and its request reading, response writing, and JSON error helpers moved into `src/net/http.c`; header names match case-insensitively, since Node's `fetch` sends `content-length`. picohttpparser remains the fallback if the Vita ever needs keep-alive, pipelining, or chunked bodies, which would happen if option B is chosen.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: feat(shell): one LAN Listener for upload and link, on from startup
lines.text: - **Credentials.** v1 trusts the LAN, like **Runtime Upload**. A linked companion answers only its Vitas, loopback and its own addresses, but IPs can be spoofed. That is harmless for reading stats, but not for typing keys or launching apps, so a credential decision must come before the first plugin that acts on the computer.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: feat(host-control): built-in plugins, .vdplugin files, vitadeck-host-companion
lines.text: - **Publishing.** `@vitadeck/host-companion` is built as a dependency-free package but stays private until its first release; until then `pnpm --dir js host-companion` runs it from a checkout.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: docs(adr): host control sliced delivery and topology (#70)
lines.text: - **Internet or account pairing.** Host Control is LAN only.

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: docs(adr): host control sliced delivery and topology (#70)

lines.author: Máté Molnár
lines.summary: feat(shell): one LAN Listener for upload and link, on from startup
lines.text: **Host Control Link** is not **Upload Pairing**. A link exchanges an address and authorizes nothing. **Upload Pairing** is a future, ephemeral credential for the **LAN Listener**, so it would guard links as well as uploads. Commands sent to the companion need their own credential; the likely shape is the same idea, a short-lived code shown on the Vita and entered on the companion. At that point, either widen **Upload Pairing** to cover both directions or add a sibling term. Decide then; do not overload the term now.

lines.summary: feat(shell): one LAN Listener for upload and link, on from startup
lines.text: **Considered options:** rebase #16 (rejected: four months stale, and it couldn't be reviewed as one change). Topology A, where the user types the computer's address on the Vita (rejected: wrong pairing direction, and it needs a Shell text editor). Topology B (see the alternative above). A second HTTP client on `sceHttp` (rejected: `fetch()` already covers it). A fixed command catalogue or a shell-command endpoint (rejected: see plugins above).
